what_its_for: Glycopyrrolate is used to treat stomach ulcers by reducing stomach acid. It is also used to control drooling in children with certain nerve conditions, and some forms are inhaled to help open the airways and make breathing easier in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It may also be used before surgery to reduce saliva and other secretions.
how_to_take: Take the tablet or liquid form by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but try to take it at the same times each day. For the inhaled form, use the inhaler device exactly as shown to you by your pharmacist or doctor — do not swallow the capsules meant for inhalation. Do not take more than prescribed, and do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
dosing: Your dose depends on why you are taking this medicine, your age, and your overall health. For stomach ulcers in adults, a common dose is 1 to 2 mg taken two to three times a day. For drooling in children, the dose is based on body weight. For the inhaled form for COPD, the usual dose is one capsule inhaled once or twice daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the liquid form tightly closed and away from light. Store inhaler capsules in their original packaging and only remove one capsule right before use. Keep all forms of this medicine away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require sharp focus until you know how this medicine affects you, because it can cause blurred vision and dizziness. Avoid alcohol, as it can increase side effects like drowsiness and dizziness. Avoid becoming overheated or dehydrated — this medicine reduces sweating, which can make it harder for your body to cool down. Avoid taking antacids at the same time as your glycopyrrolate dose unless your doctor says it is okay, as they can reduce how well the medicine is absorbed.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: difficulty urinating or no urination at all; fast or irregular heartbeat; severe constipation or bloating; eye pain or sudden vision changes; confusion or unusual behavior; signs of overheating such as hot, dry skin with no sweating and a high body temperature; a severe allergic reaction including hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also contact your doctor if side effects like dry mouth, blurred vision, or dizziness are bothering you or not going away.
when_it_works: For stomach ulcers, you may start to notice improvement within a few days to a couple of weeks of regular use. For controlling drooling, improvement is usually noticed within a few weeks. For COPD, the inhaled form starts to open the airways within about 15 to 30 minutes after use, but it is a long-term maintenance medicine and should be used every day as prescribed, not just when you feel short of breath.
special_populations: Older adults are more sensitive to the side effects of this medicine, especially confusion, urinary problems, constipation, and falls — use with caution. Children: the liquid form (Cuvposa) is approved for children aged 3 to 16 years for drooling, with doses carefully calculated by weight. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should talk to their doctor before using this medicine, as safety has not been fully established. People with glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, urinary blockage, myasthenia gravis, or severe heart disease should tell their doctor before starting this medicine, as it may not be safe for them.
